name: esedb_query
description: Read an ESE database (WebCacheV01.dat, SRUDB.dat, spartan.edb) as TABLES through esedbexport: list the tables, or return the rows of one, each row numbered by its position in the exported file. It exports tables as text and decodes nothing: a SRUM table is not joined to the application or user it names, a WebCache container is not resolved, and an ESE log is not read. The export is made once per database into esedb-export/<db sha256, first 16 hex>/ under the job's $OUT (or the agent's work directory), with the exporter's whole stdout and stderr in files beside it and an export-manifest.json (database digest, exporter version, argv, exit status, every table file); a complete export is reused by later calls only when its manifest was written by this version, its exit status was 0, and every table file it lists is on disk with its recorded size and nothing else is there (otherwise it is exported again). An exporter that exits non-zero or is stopped by export_timeout_seconds leaves a PARTIAL export: status partial, complete false, the tables listed only as tables_in_partial_export, never as the database's tables. A table name that matches more than one export file is refused with the candidates. The table file is read as the exporter wrote it, as tab-separated text with a row to a line and no quoting rule (a quote or a carriage return is a character of its cell), and _row is the 1-based line of the row after the header. A column name that repeats, or is named like a key the answer adds (_row), is numbered. What an answer prints inline is bounded: the rows that fit limit and 256 KiB, with a cell longer than 4,096 characters shown cut (_cells_shortened names it); every row, with its cells as the boundary shows them (sealed like the inline rows), is in the JSON Lines file all_results names, and the cells whole are in the export (export_dir), written whenever the inline rows are not the whole of the table, and never replaced by another result. A row longer than 8 MiB is read to that length and said to be cut (it is whole in the export). The tool stops at its own time limit (285 seconds) with the rows read and says partial. Every answer carries status (complete, partial, failed) and status_basis. SENSITIVE: the export directory holds every table whole, so whatever the database holds (a WebCache URL with a token, SRUM users, the password material of an Active Directory database, which NTDS.dit is): it is made mode 0700 with files 0600, is a sensitive output of the job that made it, and is cited by file and table, never by value; run it as a job with secret_output: true when the case may. The rows returned withhold, with a marker holding only the length, the cells of a column whose name says password, secret, token, encrypted, credential, a card, an IBAN or an SSN, and of the datatable attributes that carry password hashes, their history, supplemental credentials and the password encryption keys (columns_withheld lists them); the credential-named query and fragment parameters of a URL in a cell, and a password in its user-info, are withheld the same way, by parameter name and shape (url_secrets_withheld lists them; a secret in a URL's path or in a title, a user-info token of another shape such as one holding a slash, and free text are NOT covered and are printed; write_url_secrets: true writes the whole text of the URLs withheld to a 0600 file under $OUT, in a job only). Binary cells are exported as hex text, decoded and judged by their printable text; a WebCache header column can still hold a cookie that is not secret-shaped: cite, do not copy. The program runs in the tool's own process group (never a session of its own), so the harness ending the tool ends it; the tool's own deadline kills it and what it started, and SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP do the same and the answer is then status interrupted. WITHHOLDING (one boundary on every way out). Table names, export file names and the sizes per table are listed in the order of the text shown for each, withheld names in an order of their own that is new for every run, so that the order does not give away the order of the names themselves. Every key and value of the answer, and every row of every file this tool writes, is judged by the type of the field it fills (table names, column names and cells): a name, path, key or URL is shown as it is only when it fits a plain grammar (a path component by component; GUIDs, SIDs, addresses, 0x numbers, times and hexadecimal ids up to 24 digits are plain), free text has token-shaped runs, user-info, the value after a secret's name, vendor-prefixed tokens, padded base64 and PEM keys withheld, and a second check written apart from the first reads it all once more, the text as the evidence wrote it as well as the text shown (a piece of 12 characters of a secret that two cuts left behind is caught) (a string it replaces makes a complete answer partial and is listed under boundary.replaced_at, by the keys on the way as they are shown or by positions, never by a withheld key). A withheld text is <withheld N characters: reason>. When any part of a free-text string is withheld, the line breaks, tabs and invisible characters of that string are not kept in the text shown (it is judged without them); a string with nothing withheld is shown exactly as it is. Binary data written as hexadecimal is decoded and judged by its printable text, by both layers and by the backstop on its own; hexadecimal with no secret-shaped text in it is shown as it is, random bytes included (a binary key is printed). write_values: true writes the originals of everything withheld to <tool>-values.jsonl (mode 0600, created first, never replaced) and is accepted only in a job the harness runs as secret output (the manifest declares it; SECRET_OUTPUT=1), refused as JSON anywhere else before anything is made. Measured on random plants of every shape in 13 slots (988 per shape, five independent runs, 4,940 per shape; rates, not guarantees; the tests plant them again): prefixed tokens (GitHub, GitLab, Stripe, SendGrid, Google, npm, AWS key ids), JWT, PEM keys (one line and several), connection strings, user-info (an @, a / or a + inside the password, a random user of any length, a GitLab token glued to hexadecimal digits), NUL, zero-width and full-width splits, upper-case and glued prefixes: 0 printed whole in 4,940 plants of each shape and no piece of 12 characters of one printed; AWS-shaped secret keys of 40 characters: 0 whole and 1 piece of 12 characters in 4,940 (an earlier measurement found 2 whole and 3 pieces in 4,940, so the rate is small and not zero). The shapes that are not zero, as the range of the five runs over all slots with the worst single slot (76 plants, one plant is 1.3%) beside it: 16, 20 and 32-byte base64 keys 0.0% to 0.3% (worst slot 1.3%; up to 3.9% in end-to-end runs); random base62 of 20 to 40 characters 0.0% to 0.3% (worst slot 2.6%); random lower-case letters of 24 9.2% to 10.6% (worst slot 14.5% to 21.1%); a 16-character base32 seed 9.8% to 11.7% (worst slot 15.8% to 21.1%). In a binary slot (a hexadecimal REG_BINARY value or table cell) the backstop decodes the hexadecimal and replaces every hex-encoded shape it claims (480 of 480 plants), but random bytes that hold no text are printed (200 of 200), and so is a hexadecimal secret written as text there (a 32-digit one in a table cell: 97%). Strings changed (any part withheld) on real evidence: in a real 72 MB SOFTWARE hive (3,000 strings sampled per class) 3.7% of key-name components, 1.0% of value names and 0.9% of REG_SZ data (the names of the Windows component store, WinSxS, are not replaced by the backstop in a name, key or path); in real event logs (175 logs, 64,716 records, up to 4 MB each) the XML of 2.0% of the records is replaced whole by the backstop (5.6% before the shape guard of this round; Security 0.1%, was 6.7%), 1.7% of the data fields are withheld (3.7% before, process ids no longer) and 45 of the 175 runs end partial (84 before). Strings the shape rules change that are not secrets: numbers of 19 digits or more (handles, a Chrome field-trial handle, a mojo pipe name), unlabelled hexadecimal runs of 32 digits or more (the native-image directories), and the query values of a URL in a URL slot. NOT recognised, by design: a secret that does not look like one (a plain password or passphrase, a pronounceable passphrase, a UUID-shaped key, a hexadecimal secret of up to 24 digits in a name or of any length in a binary slot, anything under 16 characters in a name; 69% to 100% of such plants are printed): withholding is by shape, so a file whose secrets matter is read in a job run with secret_output: true.

table.description: Table to read; omit to list the tables

limit.description: Rows shown inline at most (default 200, at most 20000, an inline page size; the inline rows are also held to 256 KiB, so fewer may be shown); every row is kept whole, and when the inline rows are not the whole table the whole list is written as JSON Lines and named in all_results

export_timeout_seconds.description: How long to let esedbexport run (default 240, at most 270); a run that is stopped keeps what it wrote and the answer says partial

write_url_secrets.description: Write the whole text of every URL whose secrets were withheld, with the secret value, to a file under $OUT (mode 0600, created first, never replaced): only in a job run with secret_output: true, refused anywhere else; default false

write_values.description: Write the originals of everything the boundary withheld to a file under $OUT (mode 0600, created first, never replaced): only in a job run with secret_output: true, refused anywhere else; default false
